intro: Kisantu is a town in Kongo Central, in the hills south-west of Kinshasa, known for the botanic garden a Jesuit brother began at its mission around 1900. Among the garden's big trees stands a kapok whose trunk splits into tall flat buttresses, which a reader photographed and sent to us. We do not yet know its age or its size.

question_context: A reader sent us this kapok, Ceiba pentandra, from the botanic garden at Kisantu in Kongo Central. The garden was begun at the Jesuit mission by Brother Justin Gillet at the turn of the twentieth century and is one of the oldest in Central Africa. The photograph shows a huge pale grey trunk, still dotted with the short thorns kapoks carry, opening low down into great flat buttresses that run out over the ground like the fins of a rocket, taller than a person. The garden has put a small label at its foot naming the species. Kapoks are the trees whose seed pods give the silky fibre once used to stuff lifejackets and pillows, and they are among the tallest trees of African forests. We do not know when this one was planted, how tall it is or how wide its buttresses spread. If you visit, walk round it: each side shows a different set of fins. We have not confirmed the garden's opening hours or fees, so ask at the gate.

trees.story:
A reader sent us this kapok from the botanic garden at Kisantu, in the hills south-west of Kinshasa, and the photograph needs little explaining.

The trunk is enormous and pale grey, still dotted with the short thorns kapoks carry, and low down it opens into great flat buttresses that run out over the ground like the fins of a rocket. They are as tall as a person and taller, smooth and ribbed, and the whole base is wide enough that a group sat on chairs in its shade when the reader was there. The garden has put a small label at its foot: Ceiba pentandra, the kapok, the tree whose seed pods give the silky fibre once used to stuff lifejackets and pillows.

Kisantu's garden was begun by a Jesuit brother at the mission at the turn of the twentieth century, and many of its big trees date from its early decades. We do not know when this one was planted, or how big it is. If you know, or if you measure it, tell us here and we will add your figures.

Walk round it slowly; every side shows a different set of buttresses.
